claims.text: Exceptional hardness and strength in HEAs are primarily governed by lattice-distortion strengthening.
Atomic-size mismatches in a random solid solution create local lattice strain fields.
Local strain fields caused by atomic-size mismatch hinder dislocation motion.
Hindering dislocation motion increases resistance to plastic deformation.
The proposed baseline is a single-phase equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi solid solution with uniform grain size and minimal second-phase precipitation.
Partial substitution with a larger-sized element such as Al or Cu can be used to increase atomic-size mismatch.
The comparison should hold processing conditions and grain size constant while composition is varied.
The compared alloys must remain homogeneous and single-phase under ambient conditions.
XRD line broadening and TEM can quantify the relevant lattice distortions.
Grain size, texture, and precipitation should be controlled so that their strengthening contributions do not confound the comparison.
Enhanced lattice distortion produces local stress fields that impede dislocation slip.
Increased atomic-size mismatch increases lattice strain and the energy barrier for dislocation glide.
A higher barrier to dislocation glide produces higher hardness and yield strength than in alloys with lower lattice distortion.
HEAs having greater measured atomic-size mismatch and lattice distortion will show increased hardness and yield strength relative to the baseline.
Hardness and yield strength will vary roughly monotonically with lattice distortion over the composition range that remains single-phase.
Lattice-distortion strengthening is expected to dominate only in single-phase solid solutions with controlled microstructure.
If increasing atomic-size mismatch induces second-phase precipitation or significant grain growth, strengthening can no longer be attributed solely to lattice distortion.
Processing variations, grain-boundary strengthening, and precipitation strengthening may alter the quantitative relationship between mismatch, lattice distortion, and mechanical properties.
The hypothesis is to be rejected if the modified alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in lattice distortion together with increased hardness and strength relative to the baseline.
